aliases: Recover a hidden network only with its calibrated intervention and capacity premises An irreducible symmetric SPD M-matrix A is exactly reconstructed from n(n+1)/2 labeled scalar port responses to baseline, single shunts t/2t and pair shunts t, t>0. The inverse-M inequalities uniquely select the pair root. For K+sC with unknown positive internal shunt gains h_i, independently known diagonal C and two distinct positive real Laplace points identify all gains and K using n(n+1) scalar responses. Unknown C preserves the congruence ambiguity. Known node count/labels and calibrated positive shunts for finite tomography; exact responses and connected SPD M-matrix. Self-calibration additionally needs independent absolute capacities, common known source/port calibration, h_0=1 and exact positive-real Laplace responses. These are not two sinusoidal frequencies. Exact real identifiability/count optimality does not imply robust physical recovery. Positive diagonal shunts cannot remove the hidden-loss depth barrier under the specified readout model. The stronger transient all-signed-input bound charges squared input, not physical work. Unequal-variance extension compares Gaussian KL, not Blackwell order. All8 noisy direct calibrations rejected or left the physical class; ordinary constrained joint fitting was stronger but small port error did not identify internal parameters. No acquired measurement, fabricated device, historical priority, efficient algorithm or practical advantage is inferred from these mathematical/model results. Mission NOT_ACHIEVED.

## Model

Let A be a real symmetric positive definite n by n matrix with nonpositive
offdiagonal entries and a connected offdiagonal graph. Thus A is an irreducible
symmetric nonsingular M-matrix. A physically familiar subclass is

    A = L_w + diag(g),   w_ij >= 0, g_i >= 0,

with a connected conductance graph and at least one positive grounded leak.
A steady unit current or heat input at labeled node 0 gives temperature or
voltage vector A^{-1} e_0. The sole measured scalar is the response at node 0.
The permitted intervention adds a *known, calibrated* shunt at a selected node:

    f_A(d) = e_0^T (A + diag(d))^{-1} e_0,  d_i >= 0.

The construction assumes the number of nodes, their intervention labels and
the shunt amplitudes are known. It does not assume the graph or its weights.
The steady model requires settling after every configuration. Wiring, switches,
calibration and settling are acquisition resources; they are not supplied by
the proof. In a thermal dynamic model A(s)=K+sC, changing a heat capacity has
no steady effect at s=0. That initial idea was therefore replaced by shunts.

## Theorem 1: exact finite tomography

For every A in this class and every fixed t>0, the following d=n(n+1)/2
exact scalar measurements determine every entry of A:

* baseline d=0;
* d=t e_i and d=2t e_i for every i=1,...,n-1;
* d=t e_i+t e_j for every 1<=i<j<=n-1.

No spectral simplicity, controllability, tree topology or generic weights are
needed. No infinitesimal derivative or frequency sweep is used.

### Inverse-M inequalities

Write R=A^{-1}. All entries of R are strictly positive: express A=sI-B with
B>=0 and s>rho(B), and sum the convergent nonnegative Neumann series. Graph
connectivity gives a positive walk between each pair. Principal submatrices
are again nonsingular M-matrices. Block inversion gives, for any k and i,j!=k,

    R_ij - R_ik R_kj/R_kk = (A_{not k,not k}^{-1})_ij >= 0.       (1)

This elementary identity is the sign information needed below. Positivity of
the inverse alone without the M-matrix assumption does not give (1).

### Recover diagonals and the port column

The baseline is r=R_00. For a hidden node i put a=R_0i>0 and p=R_ii>0.
The established rank-one inverse identity gives

    l_1 = r-f_A(t e_i)  = t a^2/(1+t p),
    l_2 = r-f_A(2t e_i) = 2t a^2/(1+2t p).

In particular 0<l_1<l_2<2l_1. With q=l_2/l_1,

## A. Transient and time-varying shunt stress over the full model class

Let K_0 be a symmetric positive definite irreducible M-matrix, C a fixed known
positive diagonal matrix, b=e_0 and K_1=K_0+delta e_v e_v^T, delta>0. Initially
x_h(0)=0. For a common input u(t) and a nonnegative diagonal shunt schedule
D(t), consider

    C xdot_h = -(K_h+D(t))x_h + b u(t),   y_h=b^T x_h.

Assume D is piecewise continuous, or locally integrable where the fundamental
solutions exist. The schedule may be arbitrarily fast and arbitrarily large;
giving it for free only strengthens the attempted alternative. C is fixed,
and changing C without the corresponding physical balance terms is not in
this model. The input may have either sign and belongs to L2.

Write A_h(t)=-C^{-1}(K_h+D(t)), P=delta C^{-1}e_v e_v^T>=0, and let
U_h,D(t,s) be its state transition. These transitions are entrywise nonnegative
because the generators are Metzler. Variation of constants gives

    U_0,D(t,s)-U_1,D(t,s)
      = integral_s^t U_0,D(t,r) P U_1,D(r,s) dr >= 0.          (A1)

Adding a nonnegative diagonal loss also gives

    0 <= U_h,D(t,s) <= exp[-C^{-1}K_h(t-s)]                   (A2)

entrywise, by the same variation-of-constants comparison with D=0. Substituting
both bounds into the positive product in (A1) yields

    0 <= k_D(t,s) <= k_0(t-s),                              (A3)

where k_D=b^T(U_0,D-U_1,D)C^{-1}b is the difference of the two port impulse
kernels and k_0 is the unloaded difference kernel. This is a pointwise kernel
claim, stronger than comparing a few pulses. Both systems are exponentially
stable without D; positive D preserves the comparison and cannot cause growth.

The positive integrable kernel k_0 has total mass

    integral_0^infinity k_0(t)dt
      = b^T(K_0^{-1}-K_1^{-1})b = Delta_DC.                  (A4)

For every signed u, including under a time-varying schedule,

    |y_0(t)-y_1(t)| <= (k_0 * |u|)(t),
    ||y_0-y_1||_2 <= Delta_DC ||u||_2.                       (A5)

The last step is Young's convolution inequality. With D=0 the induced L2 gain
is exactly Delta_DC: the Fourier transform obeys |Delta G(iw)|<=Delta_DC,
with equality at w=0, and arbitrarily long slowly varying inputs approach
that gain. This is the scalar positive-system result in Rantzer's established
Theorem 3. It is not a newly discovered general control principle.

The original question was complete hidden diffusion/conductance-network recovery through one boundary sensor and controlled local changes, including boundary-invisible modes. Capacity modulation correctly pivots to calibrated shunts because capacity has no steady-state effect.
